misconceptions.description: Picks any detail from the text instead of the one the question asks for
Mixes up two numbers or names in the same text
misconceptions.exampleWrong: Q: How old? A: the number of the house

teachingSuccessCriteria: Uses the question word (what, how many, what time) to choose the detail
Copies the exact word or number from the text

lesson.title: Maria and her cat
lesson.objective: Find a name, number, colour or time in a very short text by matching the question word to the right detail.

objectives: Find a name, number, colour or time in a very short text by matching the question word to the right detail.
successCriteria: Matches the question word to the detail
Answers with the exact word or number
examples: Question: How old is Maria? Look for a number.
Question: What is the cat called? Look for a name.

items.material: Maria is eight. She has a grey cat called Coco. School starts at half past eight.
Maria is eight. She has a grey cat called Coco. School starts at half past eight.

outcomes.studyNotes: When you read to find a detail, look at the question word first. What colour? Look for a colour word. How many? Look for a number. What time? Look for a time. Who? Look for a name. Then find that kind of word in the text and copy it. Do not answer with a different detail. Example: Pia has two dogs. The dogs are black. How many dogs? Two. What colour? Black. Read the question again before you answer, and check that your answer is the same kind of word.

scriptedTutor.explanation: To find a detail, read the question word first. What colour asks for a colour, how many asks for a number, what time asks for a time. Then find that kind of word in the text.
hints: Look at the question word. What kind of word do you need?
Find a number, a colour or a name in the text that matches the question.
scriptedTutor.correctFeedback: Yes, that is the right detail.
scriptedTutor.incorrectFeedback: Not quite. Check the question word and look again at the text.
scriptedTutor.closing: Good work. Match the question word to the detail.

outcomes.studyNotes: For true, false or not given, use only the text. TRUE: the text says the same thing. FALSE: the text says something different or the opposite. NOT GIVEN: the text does not say it, so you cannot know. Do not use your own ideas. Example text: Kim has a red car. Kim has a car: true. Kim has a blue car: false. Kim has a big house: not given. If the information is missing, the answer is not given, not false. Always ask: does the text say this?

scriptedTutor.explanation: Use only the text. If it says the same, the answer is true. If it says something different, the answer is false. If it does not say, the answer is not given.
hints: Find the part of the text about this sentence. Does it say the same or something different?
If you cannot find the information in the text, what is the answer?
scriptedTutor.incorrectFeedback: Not quite. Go back to the text and check what it says.
scriptedTutor.closing: Good work. Use only the text.

outcomes.studyNotes: Reference words stop us repeating nouns. He and she are for one man or one woman. It is for one thing or animal. They and them are for more than one person or thing. To find the meaning, look back at the sentence before. Find a noun that matches the pronoun: one or many, person or thing. Example: Tom bought two books. He read them at night. He means Tom, because Tom is a man. Them means the books, because it is plural. The nearest noun is not always correct.

scriptedTutor.explanation: A reference word points back to a noun. Check if it is one or many, and a person or a thing. Then find the noun that fits.
hints: Is the pronoun singular or plural?
Look at the sentence before. Which noun matches?
scriptedTutor.incorrectFeedback: Not quite. Check if the pronoun is singular or plural, then look back again.

Rejects ideas that are too general

lesson.title: Penguins
lesson.objective: Choose the sentence that gives the main idea of a short text, not a single detail or an idea that is too general.

objectives: Choose the sentence that gives the main idea of a short text, not a single detail or an idea that is too general.
successCriteria: Chooses the idea that covers all sentences
examples: A text about penguins keeping warm: main idea = Penguins have ways to stay warm.

items.prompt: What is the main idea? A) Penguins live in the cold. B) Penguins stand close together to stay warm. C) Animals need heat. Reply with the letter only.
items.material: Penguins stand in big groups when it is very cold. They push close together and take turns standing in the middle. This keeps every bird warm.

items.prompt: What is the main idea? A) Some birds cannot fly. B) Penguins eat fish. C) Penguins swim very well. Reply with the letter only.
items.material: Penguins cannot fly, but they are excellent swimmers. They move fast under water and can dive deep to catch fish.

outcomes.studyNotes: The main idea is what the whole text is about. A detail is one small fact. A general idea is too big and could be about many texts. To find the main idea, read the whole text. Ask: what do all the sentences talk about? Check each answer. If it covers only one sentence, it is a detail. If it could fit any text on the topic, it is too general. The best answer covers all the sentences. Example: Sam runs on Monday, swims on Tuesday and cycles on Friday. Main idea: Sam does a lot of sport.

scriptedTutor.explanation: The main idea covers the whole text. A detail covers one sentence. A general idea is too big. Choose the one that fits all sentences.
hints: Check every sentence. Does the answer cover all of them or just one?
Is the answer about this text, or could it be about any text on the topic?
scriptedTutor.correctFeedback: Yes, that covers the whole text.
scriptedTutor.incorrectFeedback: Not quite. Check if your answer is just a detail or too general.
scriptedTutor.closing: Good work. The main idea covers the whole text.

outcomes.title: Sequencing events with time words
outcomes.objective: Work out the order of events in a text that uses before, after, once, until and earlier, even when the order of sentences is different.

misconceptions.description: Takes the first event mentioned as the first event that happened
misconceptions.exampleWrong: "Before bed he brushed his teeth" so teeth were first

misconceptions.description: Ignores time words and takes the last event mentioned as the last that happened
misconceptions.exampleWrong: Picks the last sentence as the last event

teachingSuccessCriteria: Uses before, after, once and earlier to order events
Puts events in time order, not text order

lesson.title: Nadia's morning
lesson.objective: Work out the order of events in a text that uses before, after, once, until and earlier, even when the order of sentences is different.

objectives: Work out the order of events in a text that uses before, after, once, until and earlier, even when the order of sentences is different.
successCriteria: Does not trust the order of sentences
examples: Before the film, we ate. = We ate first, then watched the film.

items.material: Nadia drank coffee after she finished her homework. Before the homework, she walked her dog.
Nadia drank coffee after she finished her homework. Before the homework, she walked her dog.

outcomes.studyNotes: Texts do not always tell events in the order they happened. Time words show the real order. Before X, Y: Y comes first? No. Before X, Y means Y happened before X, so Y was first. After X, Y means X was first and Y came later. Once X, Y means Y came when X was finished. Earlier means at a time before. Example: Before she slept, Mia read a book. She had cooked dinner earlier. Real order: cook dinner, read, sleep. Write the events in a list in time order, then answer the question.

scriptedTutor.explanation: The order of the sentences may not be the order of the events. Use before, after and once to put the events in time order, then answer.
hints: Make a short list of the events in time order.
Which event has a time word that shows it happened earlier than the others?
scriptedTutor.correctFeedback: Yes, that is the right order.
scriptedTutor.incorrectFeedback: Not quite. Use the time words to put the events in order first.
scriptedTutor.closing: Good work. Time words show the real order.

misconceptions.exampleWrong: Picks the answer that looks similar to the word

Checks the meaning fits the whole text

lesson.title: Unknown words in a story
lesson.objective: Work out the meaning of an unknown or multi-meaning word from the words and sentences around it.

objectives: Work out the meaning of an unknown or multi-meaning word from the words and sentences around it.
successCriteria: Uses context clues to find meaning
Tests the meaning in the sentence
examples: The crowd was huge; thousands of people filled the street. Huge means very big.

items.prompt: What does "miserable" mean here? A) very happy B) very sad C) very fast. Reply with the letter only.
items.material: It rained all week and nobody visited. Joe sat alone at the window, feeling miserable.

items.material: The teacher was fair. She gave every student the same time and the same rules.

outcomes.studyNotes: When you meet a new word, do not stop. Read the sentence before and after. Look for clues: examples, opposites, reasons or explanations. Some words have more than one meaning, so check which meaning fits the text. Try your meaning in the sentence. Does it make sense? Example: The soup was bland, with no salt or spice. The clue no salt or spice shows that bland means without much taste. The most common meaning is not always the right one. Choose the meaning that fits the clues.

scriptedTutor.explanation: Look at the words around the unknown word. They give clues. Put your meaning into the sentence and check that it makes sense. Remember that some words have more than one meaning.
hints: Which words near the word give a clue?
Try your meaning in the sentence. Does it fit the story?
scriptedTutor.correctFeedback: Yes, that meaning fits the context.
scriptedTutor.incorrectFeedback: Not quite. Look for clues around the word and check the meaning fits.
scriptedTutor.closing: Good work. Use the clues around a word.

outcomes.title: Making inferences from clues
outcomes.objective: Work out what a text suggests but does not say, using clues in the text and avoiding guesses that have no support.

misconceptions.description: Answers with what the text literally says instead of what it suggests
misconceptions.exampleWrong: Repeats the notice words as the answer

misconceptions.description: Over-infers: chooses an answer with no clue in the text
misconceptions.exampleWrong: Picks an exciting but unsupported idea

teachingSuccessCriteria: Finds at least one clue in the text
Chooses the answer supported by the clue
Rejects answers with no evidence

lesson.title: Reading between the lines
lesson.objective: Work out what a text suggests but does not say, using clues in the text and avoiding guesses that have no support.

objectives: Work out what a text suggests but does not say, using clues in the text and avoiding guesses that have no support.
examples: He wore a coat and gloves. Inference: it was cold.

items.prompt: How does Yuki probably feel? Reply with one word: excited, nervous or sleepy?
items.material: Yuki checked her notes again and again. Her hands shook as the audience took their seats.

items.prompt: Was the shop busy? Reply yes or no.
items.material: The queue reached the door. People waited with full baskets while the staff hurried between the tills.

outcomes.studyNotes: An inference is an idea the text suggests but does not say. To infer, find clues: actions, details and word choices. Then ask what they show. Example: Mara looked at the clock and tapped her foot. The text does not say she is impatient, but the clues show it. A good inference has evidence in the text. A weak guess has none. Do not just repeat the text, and do not invent a story. Check your answer: which words in the text support it? If you cannot point to a clue, choose another answer.

scriptedTutor.explanation: An inference is not written in the text, but the clues show it. Find the clues, think about what they mean, and choose the answer the text supports.
hints: Underline the actions and details. What do they suggest?
Can you point to words in the text that support your answer?
scriptedTutor.correctFeedback: Yes, the clues support that answer.
scriptedTutor.incorrectFeedback: Not quite. Look for the clues and choose the answer they support.
scriptedTutor.closing: Good work. Infer from the clues, not from guesses.

outcomes.title: Author purpose and tone
outcomes.objective: Decide why an author wrote a text (inform, persuade, warn, complain) and what tone it has, using the language the writer chooses.
prerequisites: Knows words such as formal, angry and sarcastic

misconceptions.description: Decides the purpose from the topic only and not from the language
misconceptions.exampleWrong: A text about a library must be informing

misconceptions.description: Reads ironic or sarcastic words literally
misconceptions.exampleWrong: "Thank you so much for the delay" = grateful

teachingSuccessCriteria: Looks at commands, emotive words and facts to find purpose
Notices when praise is sarcastic
Names a tone that fits the whole text

lesson.title: Why was it written?
lesson.objective: Decide why an author wrote a text (inform, persuade, warn, complain) and what tone it has, using the language the writer chooses.

objectives: Decide why an author wrote a text (inform, persuade, warn, complain) and what tone it has, using the language the writer chooses.
examples: Buy now before it is too late! = persuade
Great, it is raining on my holiday. = sarcastic

items.prompt: Why did the writer write this text? Give one word, such as inform, persuade, warn or complain.
items.material: Don't miss our summer sale! Everything half price, this weekend only. You will not find better coats anywhere, so come early.

items.prompt: Name the writer's attitude in one word, such as sarcastic, sincere or confused.
items.material: Fantastic. The wifi has gone again, just as I started my online exam. What a lovely surprise.

outcomes.studyNotes: Authors write to inform (give facts), to persuade (make you agree or buy), to warn (stop you getting hurt) or to complain (say something is wrong). Look at the language. Facts and dates suggest inform. Commands like buy or join, and strong praise, suggest persuade. Words like danger or avoid suggest warn. Angry details suggest complain. The topic alone does not decide purpose. Tone is the writer's attitude: formal, angry, joyful, sarcastic. Sarcasm says the opposite of what is meant, such as Great, another delay. Ask whether the praise fits the situation.

scriptedTutor.explanation: Look at the language, not just the topic. Facts inform. Commands and praise persuade. Danger words warn. Angry details complain. For tone, ask if the words match the situation. If praise is used about something bad, it is sarcastic.
hints: Does the text give facts, give orders, or show anger?
Does the praise fit the situation, or does it say the opposite of what the writer feels?
scriptedTutor.correctFeedback: Yes, that fits the language of the text.
scriptedTutor.incorrectFeedback: Not quite. Check the language the writer uses, not only the topic.
scriptedTutor.closing: Good work. Purpose and tone come from the writer's language.
